idea.title: What's Actually In This Pack?

fm.title: What's Actually In This Pack?
fm.beneficiaries: Anyone buying packaged food.
fm.demo_promise: Track A: extraction and aggregation, with documents and a spreadsheet of results. Track B: a working prototype. Teams may attempt either or both; each track is judged on its own merits — breadth is not rewarded, depth is.

idea.body:
Problem

Every packaged food sold in India carries a legally complete label, but interpreting it is left to the shopper — impossible for someone with lower literacy or no intent to read labels. It is a translation-and-presentation problem, which is to say a UX problem. Assume a low-end Android phone, patchy connectivity, a noisy shop aisle, three seconds of attention and one free hand.

Proposed solution

Handle at least two of the things labels hide: sugar as an abstraction (normalise independently of a manufacturer-chosen serving size, keep added sugar distinct from intrinsic); ingredient splitting (re-aggregate sugars, refined flours, fats and salts into families and re-sort — the hardest and most valuable part); category truth (an ice cream that is legally a frozen dessert); claim contradiction; opaque and animal-derived additives; sodium; and unrealistic serving sizes.

What they said they'd demo

Track A: extraction and aggregation, with documents and a spreadsheet of results. Track B: a working prototype. Teams may attempt either or both; each track is judged on its own merits — breadth is not rewarded, depth is.

Notes

Explicit anti-patterns in the submission: barcode lookup into an existing database; a red/amber/green dial nobody reads correctly; three paragraphs of LLM nutrition advice; a demo that works only on the two tested packs; an output that cannot expand "6 tsp total sugars" back into the six listed ingredients; and moral scoring or shaming. Track B requires testing on people outside the team, recording whether the choice switched, how long it took, the reason in their own words, and at least one case where the output misled someone.

update.body:
What we did

Declared demo-ready. What is actually serving, verified against the running instance rather than asserted:

  • Farmer flow — crop-opportunity score computed live from a four-component formula, so acreage, irrigation and the rainfall slider all reach it. Scores differentiate across crops (Soybean 73 to Maize 54 for Nashik in June) and the slider moves monotonically across its whole range.

  • RAG — 348 embedded chunks from TNAU crop production guides at 1024 dimensions.
  • Backend — 101 tests passing, 1 xfail (a known RAG gap, pinned deliberately).

What broke

Nothing new. But five things are knowingly open going into the demo, and a demo-ready flag with no caveats would read as a finished product:

  1. Pune ranks Cotton at 100% opportunity. Two migrations are written and reviewed but not applied, so 29 crop_market_data rows still carry a placeholder 1-quintal demand against zero supply — producing a maximum-possible demand-gap ratio for crops ICRISAT reports as not grown in that district. This one is on screen if anyone picks Pune.
  2. The sources panel renders empty — all 13 fertilizer_recommendations rows have a NULL source_id.
  3. RAG can answer one crop's question from another crop's document. Ask-mode retrieves with no crop filter. Chunks are tagged with crop_id, so the fix is a filter, not re-ingestion.
  4. The 7-day weather outlook is always blank — weather_forecast is empty and no weather API is wired up.
  5. First recommendation takes ~2.5s — 40+ sequential queries over an ngrok tunnel. Not a code path problem; the pool was retuned to stop it failing under a retry burst, which is different from making it fast.

Nothing new this record. Status change only.

update.body:
What we did

Two layers, deliberately different in kind.

Job 1 — nightly fertilizer-demand forecast. XGBoost over a pooled panel built from 4,598 real sales rows, writing forecast and recommendations for the business dashboard. Forecasts at district x quarter and allocates down to product-month; intervals are recalibrated from held-out residuals rather than trusted from the model's quantile heads. Runs as one flocked nightly script.

Job 2 — live crop-opportunity score. A deterministic weighted formula, not a model, so the farmer's acreage, irrigation answer and rainfall slider all reach it at request time. Four components at 0-100, each returned separately with a plain-language reason. Confidence is a second, independent number.

What broke

Three things, all user-visible, none of which errored:

  1. The rainfall slider was inert across its whole UI range. Threshold-based scoring.
  2. Every crop in a district got an identical weather score — same root cause, the function took no crop argument.
  3. The same crop showed different scores on the list and its own detail page, because the detail endpoint ignored sowing_month and silently scored a different month.

Also found and fixed: quantity_mt / forecast_mt / current_stock_mt on the business API were a 1000x mislabel — the pipeline produces packets, not metric tons — on fields feeding a dispatch decision.

What we decided

The three linked decisions. The one worth reading is the granularity choice: the table's declared shape was treated as a specification, and measuring first showed it could not be honoured honestly.

What we'd tell another team attempting this

Compute the stupid baseline before you believe your model — predicting zero scored 100% and our "winning" model scored 97.6%. Sweep the range of any control you ship, because a slider that returns 200 and a plausible number on every drag looks fine until someone drags it twice. And when an AI sources domain data you cannot check by eye, run a second pass told to refute rather than review: ours produced 22 corrections, and the worst error was the one the first pass had explicitly justified.

decision.title: Score crop opportunity for farmers with a deterministic weighted formula, not a trained model

fm.decision: Score crop opportunity for farmers with a deterministic weighted formula, not a trained model

options_considered.option: Train a model on the same panel the fertilizer forecast uses
options_considered.why_not: A model fitted last night cannot see what the farmer typed this morning. The form collects acreage and irrigation, and the what-if screen lets them drag a rainfall slider — none of which reaches a nightly artifact. It would also inherit the same sparsity that made product-month forecasting noise.

options_considered.option: Serve a nightly-precomputed score per district/crop/month
options_considered.why_not: Same problem in cheaper form. Precomputation cannot respond to a slider, and the slider is the demo's headline interaction.

fm.chosen_because: The farmer's own inputs are the most informative signal available, and they only exist at request time. A formula recomputes from them instantly, and every term can be shown to the farmer and argued with — four components at 0-100 (weather fit 35%, demand vs supply 30%, demand trend 20%, stability 15%), each returned separately with a plain-language reason.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: Gives up any ability to learn interactions the weights do not encode. The weights are a judgement call, not a fit — they live as one named constant block so they are visibly tunable rather than buried.
fm.revisit_if: Enough labelled outcome data accumulates to fit crop-choice outcomes rather than assert weights — i.e. once actual farmer results, not just intents, are recorded.

decision.body:
Context

Two jobs looked similar and are not. Predicting next month's fertilizer demand for the business is a batch forecasting problem. Scoring which crops are worth growing for a specific farmer is an interactive one.

Options

As above. The deciding question was not "which is more accurate" but "which can see the farmer's answers at all".

Rationale

Confidence is reported as a second, separate number — how much real data sits behind the score — so "high opportunity, low confidence" stays sayable. Folding it into the score would have hidden exactly the cases worth flagging. It currently caps at 70% because ACTUAL production data covers only 2016-17, and five crops have none at all.

Consequences

Scores differentiate meaningfully across crops for the first time (Soybean 73 down to Maize 54 for Nashik in June), and the rainfall slider moves. The per-crop agronomic bands the weather term needs had to be sourced separately — see the ETc decision and the adversarial-pass learning.

decision.title: Express every crop's water requirement as ETc (crop evapotranspiration) rather than field water requirement, and correct the one crop that had been sourced the other way

fm.decision: Express every crop's water requirement as ETc (crop evapotranspiration) rather than field water requirement, and correct the one crop that had been sourced the other way

options_considered.option: Keep the figure each source reported most naturally
options_considered.why_not: Breaks cross-crop comparability, which is the only thing the score uses the number for. Paddy was sourced as 900-1400 mm FIELD water — which correctly includes puddling plus seepage and percolation — while every other crop was 250-700 mm ETc. Scoring rice against that band would have made it unrecommendable in every district, on a units mismatch rather than on agronomy.

options_considered.option: Convert field water to ETc ourselves
options_considered.why_not: Requires assumptions about percolation rates on black cotton soil that we cannot source, so it would replace a visible error with an invisible one.

fm.chosen_because: The score compares one crop's water need against one district-month's rainfall, so the only property that matters is that all 13 crops are measured the same way. ETc is the figure FAO publishes per crop and the one the other 12 were already on.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: The rice figure now understates what a farmer must actually supply to a puddled paddy field, because puddling and percolation are excluded. Acceptable for ranking crops against each other; not a basis for sizing irrigation.
fm.revisit_if: The score ever drives an irrigation-volume recommendation rather than a crop ranking, at which point field water becomes the correct figure and every crop needs re-sourcing on that basis.

decision.body:
Context

The farmer-facing weather term needs, per crop, an ideal temperature band and a water requirement. Thirteen crops were sourced against FAO, ICAR, MPKV, Dr. PDKV and TNAU references.

Options

As above.

Rationale

The error was found by an independent verification pass instructed to refute rather than confirm, and it was the only MAJOR finding among 13 crops. It is a good example of a defect that reads as diligence: the original figure was correctly sourced, correctly cited, and explicitly justified in the researcher's own notes — it was simply the wrong quantity for this comparison.

Consequences

Rice moved from 900-1400 to 450-700, and all 13 crops now sit between 87 and 159 mm/month derived need. A unit-guard test now fails any requirement whose monthly need exceeds 250 mm, so this specific mistake cannot return silently.

decision.title: Forecast fertilizer demand at district x quarter and allocate down to product-month, rather than forecasting district x product x month directly

fm.decision: Forecast fertilizer demand at district x quarter and allocate down to product-month, rather than forecasting district x product x month directly

options_considered.option: Forecast district x product x month directly, the granularity the forecast table declares
options_considered.why_not: Measured on a 2024 holdout it carries no signal. Seasonal-naive scored 136.8% WAPE and XGBoost 97.6%, against 100.0% for predicting zero — so the model only "won" by hedging everything toward zero (bias -35.3 packets/cell). 144 series average 10.2 observed months each out of 60; 63 of them have fewer than 6.

options_considered.option: Forecast district x category x month, then split to product by mix share
options_considered.why_not: 102.9% WAPE — still worse than predicting nothing. Category is denser than product (41 series, 22.5 months average) but monthly is still too fine.

options_considered.option: Forecast state total x quarter, the strongest signal available (24.7% WAPE)
options_considered.why_not: Too coarse to serve the business dashboard, which queries by district_id. More of the final number would be allocation than forecast.

fm.chosen_because: District x quarter is the finest granularity where a model beats its own baseline by a real margin — 57.6% WAPE against 72.2% seasonal-naive. Everything finer was measured first and rejected on the numbers, not on taste.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: Every per-product monthly row written to the forecast table is an ALLOCATION of a coarser forecast, not a forecast at that granularity. Accepted only because forecast.confidence carries the word "Allocated" on all 2,898 rows and recommendations.reason repeats it in full, so no consumer can mistake one for the other.
fm.revisit_if: More Sales_Bio history lands, or more districts are onboarded. The binding constraint is 4,598 real sales rows over 5 years across 7 districts and 25 products — not the choice of model.

decision.body:
Context

schema.sql reserves forecast and recommendations for a batch ML job and the business dashboard reads them directly, so the table's own granularity — (district, product, year, month) — looked like the specification. Three dashboard panels were empty until something filled it.

Options

The three above, all evaluated on the same 2024 holdout with the same features. The baseline was built before any model, which is the only reason the failure was visible: a 97.6% WAPE reads like a working model until you notice predicting zero scores exactly 100%.

Rationale

Aggregation was pushed upward only as far as it had to go. Measured seasonal-naive WAPE by level: district x product x month 135.9%, district x category x month 129.3%, product x month 108.5%, district x month 94.9%, category x month 81.6%, district x quarter 72.2%, state x quarter 24.7%. District x quarter is where a trained model first earns its place.

Consequences

The nightly job writes 2,898 allocated rows for 2025-2026 and the three dead dashboard panels populate. The honesty cost is carried by the confidence column rather than by a footnote. Sales data ends 2024-12, so 2026 rows are a 7-8 quarter extrapolation and are labelled Allocated: Very Low.

decision.title: Make decisions and learnings first-class entities, not a record_kind inside updates

fm.decision: Make decisions and learnings first-class entities, not a record_kind inside updates

options_considered.option: Type them inside update files as record_kind: decision | learning
options_considered.why_not: Fewer shapes for a contributor to learn, but a decision buried in a day's status blob is unfindable — no cross-team query, and no way to supersede one without rewriting the update it sat in.

fm.chosen_because: A decision is addressable, individually promotable into tekdibraincore, and can be superseded on its own. 'Show me every model-choice across all nine teams' becomes a grep.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: Two more entity shapes. Mitigated by the contributor never filling them by hand — the assistant does, from conversation.
fm.revisit_if: Contributors start writing updates and skipping decisions because the extra shape is friction.

decision.body:
Context

The whole premise — Idea 20 — is that delivery decisions are the asset and they currently evaporate. Filing them inside status updates would have reproduced exactly the problem being solved.

Rationale

Two rules do the real work and only make sense on a first-class entity: a decision needs at least one rejected option with a reason, and a learning needs evidence and a cost. Both are enforced by the validator.

Consequences

Team 7 has since logged two decisions and two learnings of its own in this shape.

decision.body:
Context

An empty repo and a live 48-hour event. The company brain's model was the obvious reuse candidate.

Options

Reusing the five folders was tempting because the skill already understood them — zero new schema to learn. It fails on the central relationship: 25 ideas, 9 teams, and a many-to-one mapping between them that projects/ cannot express.

Rationale

The thing worth keeping from a hackathon is which problem statements got picked up, by whom, and what they learned. That is the mapping. A model that loses it would have been cheaper to build and worth less.

Consequences

Two schemas now exist. CONVENTIONS.md carries a promotion path — reusable work becomes an entry in tekdibraincore linking back to slugs here, never a copy.

decision.title: Reconcile teams to ideas by title-slug only; flag what does not match instead of guessing

fm.decision: Reconcile teams to ideas by title-slug only; flag what does not match instead of guessing

options_considered.option: Fuzzy-match the titles
options_considered.why_not: Two of the nine labels — 'Agritech Predictive Analytics & Intent' and 'CivicLens' — have no counterpart in the ideas sheet at all, so fuzzing would invent a nearest neighbour and it would look authoritative.

fm.chosen_because: A wrong link is worse than a missing one: nothing downstream questions it. Unmatched teams carry idea_unresolved plus the label verbatim, so somebody can ask the team.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: Two of nine teams have no idea linked, and the wiki looks incomplete until a human resolves them.
fm.revisit_if: An organiser publishes a canonical idea-number mapping.

decision.body:
Context

Seeding from two spreadsheets written at different times by different people.

decision.title: Put the entity model in a machine-readable SCHEMA.yml and write a generic validator, rather than patching the company brain's validator

fm.decision: Put the entity model in a machine-readable SCHEMA.yml and write a generic validator, rather than patching the company brain's validator

options_considered.option: Patch the existing 961-line validate_wiki.py

decision.title: Accept the record shapes contributors actually wrote, for the second time, rather than correcting their files

fm.decision: Accept the record shapes contributors actually wrote, for the second time, rather than correcting their files

options_considered.option: Enforce the documented shapes and rewrite the offending records
options_considered.why_not: Four of the five causes were the schema missing a shape, not the record being wrong. Rewriting somebody's record to satisfy a validator points the correction the wrong way, and it was their content hours before judging.

decision.body:
Context

ThreadAI's architecture update failed validation seventeen times while publish-site succeeded, so the live page was serving content the validator rejected.

The one place the rule held was inline decisions and learnings: those are a real loss of cross-team visibility, so they warn rather than pass silently or fail. Content kept, cost named.

Seventeen errors to zero. A rejected vocabulary value now names its closest match, which is what turns "'build' is not in vocabulary 'stage'" into something a contributor can act on.

decision.title: Accept the shapes contributors actually wrote — mapping-form metrics, rename tombstones — instead of correcting their files

fm.decision: Accept the shapes contributors actually wrote — mapping-form metrics, rename tombstones — instead of correcting their files

options_considered.option: Enforce the documented list form and rewrite the offending records
options_considered.why_not: Two teams independently reached for the compact mapping. That is the schema being unnatural, not two people being careless — and editing somebody's record to satisfy a validator points the correction the wrong way.

decision.body:
Context

Contributors inventing a field is a schema gap. Contributors converging on an undocumented shape is a design signal. Neither is a user error.

Schema v2, additive: team.related_ideas, idea.related_teams, team.deprecated, team.renamed_to; references resolve by bare filename as well as team/filename; metrics accept the mapping form; tombstones are exempt from the requirements of a live entity. decision.title: Compute every generated field in one shared module that both the rollup writer and the validator read

fm.decision: Compute every generated field in one shared module that both the rollup writer and the validator read

options_considered.option: Keep the rules in both scripts, as they were

decision.title: Model a project — one team's implementation of one idea — as a first-class entity, and hang every record off it

fm.decision: Model a project — one team's implementation of one idea — as a first-class entity, and hang every record off it

options_considered.option: Add an optional `idea` field to records, leaving the team as the parent
options_considered.why_not: Additive and safe, and it would have answered the filtering question today. But the pair is the thing that exists: without an object for it there is nowhere to put a status, a repo or a demo URL per piece of work, and a team with two ideas has two of each.

options_considered.option: Fix only the filtering and leave the schema
options_considered.why_not: The records carry no idea, so there is nothing to filter by. It would have been a filter over data that cannot answer the question.

Reported as a UX complaint — records could not be filtered by idea. The cause was the model: update.team was required and the path to an idea ran through the team, which only works while a team has one.

decision.title: Implement the routing guard as which_brain.py instead of leaving it as instructions in SKILL.md

fm.decision: Implement the routing guard as which_brain.py instead of leaving it as instructions in SKILL.md

options_considered.option: Leave it as prose in Step 0a for the model to follow
options_considered.why_not: The failure mode is silent. A rule that depends on recall fires most of the time, and the times it does not are exactly the times nobody notices.

decision.title: Standing in an unregistered wiki writes nothing, rather than falling back to the default brain

fm.decision: Standing in an unregistered wiki writes nothing, rather than falling back to the default brain

options_considered.option: Fall back to the configured default brain
options_considered.why_not: Content plainly meant for the wiki you are standing in ends up in one with a different audience, validates cleanly there, and nothing afterwards says it is misfiled.

options_considered.option: Warn and write anyway
options_considered.why_not: Same outcome, with a message that gets skimmed. A warning is not a control.

fm.chosen_because: A refusal is loud, immediate and recoverable. A misroute is silent and permanent.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: A legitimate capture is occasionally blocked and needs the registry widened deliberately.

decision.body:
Context

Parth's constraint, stated plainly: the customer brain he is building must never be a routing target for his install or anyone's at Tekdi.

Rationale

Its absence from the registry is what enforces that — so the behaviour when standing inside it has to be refusal, not redirection. Redirecting would take customer-context content and put it in the company brain, which is the exact outcome the exclusion exists to prevent.

Consequences

Verified from the installed copy: in that repo the guard returns REFUSE, exit 3, and names the repository. In an ordinary project repo it does not fire at all.

decision.title: Ship the skill with no brain configured, and ask at install or on first use

fm.decision: Ship the skill with no brain configured, and ask at install or on first use

options_considered.option: Default to tekdi/tekdibraincore, as the skill already did
options_considered.why_not: A hackathon participant has no access to that repo. Their first capture 404s and the error looks like their own mistake — the worst possible first impression of a tool nobody asked them to install.

options_considered.option: Ask in every conversation instead of persisting an answer
options_considered.why_not: Tolerable with a shell, unusable on a chat surface, where there is nowhere to save the answer and the question therefore never stops.

decision.body:
Context

The assistant had already implemented this with [tekdibraincore, moihackathon-brain] shipped and the company brain as default.

Rationale

Parth caught it mid-implementation: hackathon participants will install this pointed only at the hackathon brain and will not have the company brain at all. The shipped default encoded an assumption about who installs the skill, and that assumption was wrong for the largest group of installers.

Consequences

install.sh asks; where it was not asked, the skill asks once on first use, verifies reachability, and offers to persist the answer. See the learning a default is an assumption about your user.

decision.title: Export the complete, secret-scrubbed project as a ZIP for manual push to a private GitHub repo, instead of an automated backup.

fm.decision: Export the complete, secret-scrubbed project as a ZIP for manual push to a private GitHub repo, instead of an automated backup.

options_considered.option: Create a new private repo and push directly via the connected GitHub App/connector
options_considered.why_not: The GitHub App installation isn't authorized to create repositories, and the connector wasn't installed with repo access for this project in this sandbox — so it authenticates but cannot create or push to a repo.

fm.chosen_because: It was the only path available to get the work off the sandbox and into the user's hands without direct GitHub write access.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: Backup requires a manual step from the user (downloading and pushing the ZIP) rather than a fully automated push, and the sandbox's local commit history isn't carried over unless the user re-initializes git before pushing.
fm.revisit_if: Once the GitHub App installation is granted repository-creation/write access for this project (or another form of repo write access is arranged).

decision.body:
Context

Needed to get a verified, secret-scrubbed backup of the full Joomla2Node project out of the sandbox and into a private GitHub repo, but had no direct git/GitHub write access from the sandbox environment.

Options

Direct push via the GitHub App/connector was the natural first choice but was blocked by permissions — see options_considered.

Rationale

Exporting a ZIP was the only remaining path that didn't require GitHub write access, and the export was verified clean on a secret scan before handoff.

Consequences

decision.title: Split the migration guidance into 17 separate per-stage skills (00 overview + 01-16 stages) rather than one large end-to-end migration skill.

fm.decision: Split the migration guidance into 17 separate per-stage skills (00 overview + 01-16 stages) rather than one large end-to-end migration skill.

options_considered.option: One large single SKILL.md covering the entire 16-stage pipeline
options_considered.why_not: Claude's skill-loading model favors small, focused files (progressive disclosure) — a single monolithic file would force loading the whole pipeline's instructions even when only one stage is relevant, and would make it impossible for a "run complete migration" skill to orchestrate the others without duplicating their content inline.

fm.chosen_because: Per-stage skills let an agent load only the stage it's working on, let the orchestration skill (16) reference the other 15 without repeating their instructions, and let each stage be independently inspected and audited — which is exactly how 6 real defects were caught before delivery.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: 17 separate files instead of 1 means more surface area to keep mutually consistent and in sync with the underlying engine as it evolves — cross-skill consistency has to be actively audited rather than being automatically true of a single file.
fm.revisit_if: Maintaining consistency across 17 files under source drift becomes more costly than the modularity is worth, or Claude's skill-loading model changes to better support large multi-section files.

decision.body:
Context

Needed to package the already-implemented Joomla2Node engine into skill(s) an AI agent could follow to migrate an arbitrary Joomla extension, without duplicating or modifying the engine itself.

Options

A single monolithic skill covering all 16 stages was the natural first shape but was rejected — see options_considered.

Rationale

Per-stage skills support progressive disclosure, let the orchestration skill reference rather than repeat the others, and make each stage independently auditable.

Consequences

17 files now need to be kept consistent with each other and with the real source as the engine changes; an independent audit pass is the mitigation, and it already proved its worth by catching 6 defects in the first pass.

learning.title: AI-sourced domain data needs a second pass instructed to REFUTE, not review. The refute framing caught errors that were correctly sourced, correctly cited, and explicitly justified by the first pass.

fm.learning: AI-sourced domain data needs a second pass instructed to REFUTE, not review. The refute framing caught errors that were correctly sourced, correctly cited, and explicitly justified by the first pass.
fm.evidence: Sourcing ideal temperature and water ranges for 13 crops ran as 4 research agents followed by 4 independent verification agents told to consult sources themselves and try to refute the figures (8 agents, 622K tokens, 335 tool calls, 0 errors). The verify pass produced 22 corrections. One was MAJOR — rice reported at 900-1400 mm field water against 450-700 mm ETc for every other crop, which would have made paddy unrecommendable everywhere on a units mismatch. It also cut Potato's band by ~40% (500-700 to 350-500), RAISED Chilli's (600 to 700 max — the one error pointing in the dangerous direction, toward under-watering advice), downgraded Grapes from "sourced" to "uncertain" because the lower bound could not be traced, and flagged a real MPKV document that did not say what the first pass claimed it said.
fm.generalises_to: Any AI-generated factual table that will be trusted at face value downstream, especially domain data a reviewer cannot check by eye. "Review this" and "try to refute this" produce measurably different results from the same model on the same input — the second finds errors the first rationalises. Pair it with a schema that carries per-row certainty so an unsourced figure cannot silently read like a sourced one.
fm.would_do_differently: Ask the research pass for the QUANTITY definition explicitly (ETc vs field water) rather than a bare number with units. The rice error was a units-semantics failure, not a lookup failure, and a required "what exactly does this figure measure" field would have surfaced it in the first pass instead of the second.
fm.cost_of_lesson: 622K tokens and about 30 minutes wall-clock for the verification half, against shipping farmer-facing agronomic advice with a 2x error on one crop and a fabricated citation on another. The cheapest thing we did all day.

learning.body:
What happened

The crop-opportunity score needed per-crop agronomic bands. Writing 13 crops x 4 numbers from model memory would have been exactly the fabricated-agronomy failure this project had been avoiding elsewhere, so it was run as a two-phase workflow: research with real citations, then independent verification instructed to refute.

Evidence

22 corrections applied, recorded field-by-field with the disagreement text and the verifier's own sources in crop_requirements_provenance.json. Distribution of verdicts: 4 CONFIRMED, 8 MINOR_DISAGREEMENT, 1 MAJOR_DISAGREEMENT.

The MAJOR one is the instructive case. The first pass sourced it correctly, cited FAO and IRRI accurately, and wrote a note explaining precisely why it had chosen field water over ETc. It was diligent and wrong, and no amount of re-reading the first pass's own output would have caught it — the error was only visible against the other 12 crops.

What we'd do differently

Require the research pass to state what each figure measures, not just its value and unit. Also carry certainty per row — two crops ended as uncertain rather than sourced, which is more useful than a uniformly confident table.

learning.title: A model can beat its baseline and still be worse than predicting nothing — and you only see it if you compute the trivial baseline before you believe the model.

fm.learning: A model can beat its baseline and still be worse than predicting nothing — and you only see it if you compute the trivial baseline before you believe the model.
fm.evidence: On a 2024 holdout at district x product x month, seasonal-naive scored 136.8% WAPE and XGBoost 97.6%. Read alone, that is a 39-point improvement and looks like a working model. But predicting zero scores exactly 100.0% WAPE by definition, and the model's bias was -35.3 packets per cell — it had learned to hedge toward zero against a target that is 62% zeros, which is the rational move and useless for planning. The same pipeline at district x quarter scored 57.6% against a 72.2% baseline, which is a real win. Both numbers came from the same code; only the granularity differed.
fm.generalises_to: Any forecasting or scoring task on sparse or intermittent data. Compute the degenerate baselines — predict zero, predict the mean, predict last period — before the model, and report them next to it permanently. Also: prefer WAPE to MAPE on intermittent series, because MAPE divides by the actual and a single zero month makes it infinite.
fm.would_do_differently: Write the baseline script before the feature pipeline, not after. We built features first and nearly reported a 97.6% model as the deliverable; the baseline was what stopped it.
fm.cost_of_lesson: Roughly two hours of pipeline work aimed at the wrong granularity, plus the near-miss of shipping a forecast into a dashboard that presents it as fact. Cheap only because the baseline existed before anything was written to the database.

learning.body:
What happened

The forecast table declares (district, product, year, month), so that is where the first model was fitted. It beat seasonal-naive comfortably and would have been reported as working. Because a baseline module had been written first, the predict-zero reference was also on screen — at exactly 100% — which made the 97.6% legible as a failure instead of a success.

Evidence

Measured seasonal-naive WAPE by aggregation level, same holdout, same features:

levelzerosnaive WAPE
district x product x month62%135.9%
district x category x month41%129.3%
product x month27%108.5%
district x month19%94.9%
category x month4%81.6%
district x quarter4%72.2%
state total x quarter0%24.7%

Pareto did not rescue it either: the top 20 of 144 series are only 62% of volume.

What we'd do differently

Baseline first, always, and keep it in the metrics output permanently rather than as a one-off check. A model's error is meaningless without the trivial alternatives beside it.

learning.title: A scoring function built from threshold penalties made the demo's headline interaction silently inert — the rainfall slider recomputed correctly on every drag and always returned the same number.

fm.learning: A scoring function built from threshold penalties made the demo's headline interaction silently inert — the rainfall slider recomputed correctly on every drag and always returned the same number.
fm.evidence: The what-if screen offers a rainfall slider across -30% to +30%. Every stop in that range returned "No change", and testing beyond the UI range showed -100% rainfall also produced an identical score. Cause: weather suitability subtracted fixed penalties at hard rainfall thresholds (<10mm, <20mm, >250mm, >350mm), so any change that did not cross a threshold changed nothing — and Nashik's January mean of 6.4mm sits below the lowest threshold already, so nothing downward could ever move it. Replacing the thresholds with a continuous trapezoid (full marks inside the crop's ideal band, decaying linearly to zero at its absolute limits) made every step move: -30% now reads -3 to -4 points, +30% reads +2 to +3.
fm.generalises_to: Any user-facing control wired to a banded or thresholded score. The bug is invisible in code review, invisible in unit tests that assert a single value, and invisible in a demo where nobody drags the control — it only shows as "the slider does nothing", which reads as a frontend fault. Test the CONTROL's range, not the function's output at one point.
fm.would_do_differently: Write the range test at the same time as the control — assert that the endpoints of whatever the UI exposes produce different values. We now have exactly that test, plus a monotonicity test on the underlying band function, because the second-order risk is someone "simplifying" the curve back into bands.
fm.cost_of_lesson: The interaction was dead for the whole first build and nobody noticed, because the endpoint returned 200 and a plausible number every time. Found only by sweeping the slider range deliberately rather than spot-checking one value. Fix itself was under an hour once diagnosed.

learning.body:
What happened

The scenario endpoint accepted a rainfall delta, recomputed a score, and returned it. It worked in the sense that it never errored. The existing test asserted that a 0% change produced "No change" and that a 300% change produced something different — both true, and both blind to the fact that the entire range the UI actually offers produced nothing.

Evidence

Measured across the real slider range, before and after:

before -30%: No change -15%: No change 0%: No change +15%: No change +30%: No change after -30%: -3 pts -15%: -2 pts 0%: no change +15%: +2 pts +30%: +3 pts

The same fix resolved a second symptom nobody had connected to it: every crop in a district scored an identical weather value, because the function took no crop argument at all.

What we'd do differently

Two tests now guard it: one sweeps the slider's own endpoints through the API and asserts the values differ, one asserts the band function is strictly monotonic outside its plateau. A plateau inside the ideal band is correct agronomy and is deliberately kept — the bug was the discontinuity, not the flat region.

fm.would_do_differently: Avoid the reserved words entirely when naming fields — the rename cost nothing on day one and would have cost a migration later.

fm.would_do_differently: List what the hand-written version does well before replacing it, then find the structural rule that keeps each item — a single-valued field partitions a set, so it can stack; an avatar is a property the model can declare.
fm.cost_of_lesson: A full second pass, and the user having to point out that the original still looked better

Screenshots of the live original beside the rewrite: the original's one stacked bar with a legend against three plain bar charts, one of which duplicated the stage rail.

learning.title: Reading the DOM proved the data was right and said nothing about whether the page was usable

fm.learning: Reading the DOM proved the data was right and said nothing about whether the page was usable
fm.evidence: DOM assertions confirmed stat cards were anchors with correct routes, a claimed idea read In Progress, and a person's page reached their team's ideas — all true, all passing. Screenshots then showed split cards, an email rendered as a card body, an address title-cased as though it were a label, each part capitalised, every feed item printing its title twice, and a decision's rejected options crushed into a 220px sidebar in monospace.
fm.generalises_to: Any UI change verified programmatically: assertions test the contract you thought of, a screenshot tests the one you did not.
fm.would_do_differently: Screenshot every page before claiming a UI change is done, and treat 'verified in a browser' as meaning pixels rather than query results.
fm.cost_of_lesson: Six distinct defects that assertions had passed, found in one pass of screenshots

learning.title: A page can be out of date because the branch is behind or because the build artifact was not regenerated, and the two look identical

fm.learning: A page can be out of date because the branch is behind or because the build artifact was not regenerated, and the two look identical
fm.evidence: The local site was missing four teams' newest records. Two separate causes: the working branch predated four commits on main, and site/data.json — gitignored, built in CI — had last been generated two commits earlier. Merging fixed one; rebuilding fixed the other.
fm.generalises_to: Any static site generated from repository content: 'the page is stale' is two questions, and answering only one leaves it stale.
fm.would_do_differently: Check both before investigating anything else: how far behind is the branch, and when was the artifact built. The artifact records the commit it came from, which makes the second question answerable in one command.
fm.cost_of_lesson: A few minutes, and it would have been a confusing bug report from anyone else

learning.title: A shipped default is an assumption about who installs the thing, and it was wrong for the largest group of installers

fm.learning: A shipped default is an assumption about who installs the thing, and it was wrong for the largest group of installers
fm.evidence: The registry was implemented shipping `[tekdibraincore, moihackathon-brain]` with the company brain as default. Hackathon participants have no access to tekdibraincore, so every participant's first capture would have 404'd against a private repo — and the error message would have looked like their own misconfiguration. Caught by Parth mid-implementation, not by the person writing it.
fm.generalises_to: Any tool with a default target: the default encodes a belief about the median user, and that belief should be stated out loud before it is compiled in.
fm.would_do_differently: Ask who the largest group of installers is before choosing a default, and prefer shipping unconfigured when the answer differs by audience.
fm.cost_of_lesson: One implementation round reworked; caught before anything shipped

learning.body:
What happened

The assistant designed the registry around its own context — a machine with the company brain on it — and defaulted to that.

Evidence

The shipped config was repo: tekdi/tekdibraincore until Parth pointed out that participants will only ever have the hackathon brain.

What we'd do differently

The registry now ships empty, which has no default to be wrong about.

learning.title: Writing a rule as code exposed a case the prose version had silently gotten wrong

fm.learning: Writing a rule as code exposed a case the prose version had silently gotten wrong
fm.evidence: The prose said 'the working directory wins'. Implementing it forced the question of what counts as a wiki — and the first test matrix showed the naive version would refuse in every ordinary project repo, blocking all captures from application code. The fix (a wiki is a repo with CONVENTIONS.md at its root) only became visible once it had to be written down as a condition.
fm.generalises_to: Any rule stated as prose for a model to follow: implementing it is a completeness check on the rule itself, independent of whether the code ever runs.
fm.would_do_differently: Write the deterministic part first, then write the prose from it — not the other way round.
fm.cost_of_lesson: ~20 minutes, before anything was installed

learning.body:
What happened

The routing guard existed as instructions in SKILL.md. Turning it into which_brain.py required deciding what "inside a wiki" means, which the prose had left to intuition.

Evidence

First run of the matrix: an ordinary project repo would have been treated the same as a wiki, so the refusal would have fired everywhere.

What we'd do differently

Treat prose rules with a silent failure mode as unfinished until something deterministic can answer them.

learning.title: The documented cause of a connector failure was wrong, and it was asserted twice before anyone checked the API

fm.learning: The documented cause of a connector failure was wrong, and it was asserted twice before anyone checked the API
fm.evidence: USAGE.md and docs/adopting.md both said a private-repo connector failure means an org admin has not approved the OAuth app. `gh api /orgs/tekdi/installations` showed the app was installed and `repository_selection: selected` — the actual cause was simply that a newly created repo was not in the installation's list. The wrong diagnosis was given to Parth twice, including as an action item.
fm.generalises_to: Any 'ask your admin' runbook step: the API usually knows the real state, and a plausible documented cause survives unchallenged precisely because it is documented.
fm.would_do_differently: Query the state before repeating a documented diagnosis — one command would have replaced a paragraph of confident wrong advice.
fm.cost_of_lesson: ~30 minutes of wrong advice, plus doc corrections in two repositories

learning.title: Running an independent audit subagent — with no memory of how the first draft was produced — against the same real source caught 6 real defects in AI-authored skill documentation, including one outright fabricated import and a stale architecture diagram copied from a stale README, that the original drafting pass had missed.

fm.learning: Running an independent audit subagent — with no memory of how the first draft was produced — against the same real source caught 6 real defects in AI-authored skill documentation, including one outright fabricated import and a stale architecture diagram copied from a stale README, that the original drafting pass had missed.
fm.evidence: The audit subagent flagged (1) a fabricated import of functions not actually re-exported at the @joomla2node/generator package root, (2) a stale flat directory-layout diagram — copied from the generator package's own stale README — contradicted by the real generated output tree, repeated in two separate files, (3) an approximate "~70" count of a hardcoded table set that was actually exactly 64, (4) a broken cross-reference to a references/ file that doesn't exist in this skill family, (5) an overstated claim that SQL parsing captures keys/indexes when only primary-key flags are actually captured, (6) a missing Inputs/Outputs section in the orchestration skill. All 6 were independently verified against the real source and fixed before delivery.
fm.generalises_to: For any AI-authored technical documentation meant to be trusted at face value (skills, ADRs, onboarding docs), run a second, independently-instantiated review pass against the primary source before delivery — the same context that wrote the first draft is poorly positioned to catch its own fabrications, especially ones copied from other stale documentation.
fm.would_do_differently: Not stated this round.
fm.cost_of_lesson: One additional subagent pass reading the same ~15 source files fresh, plus targeted fixes to 6 files — under an hour, and cheap relative to the risk of shipping a skill that tells the next agent to import a function that doesn't exist.

learning.body:
What happened

While drafting 17 product-level Joomla2Node migration skills, an independent audit subagent — separate from and with no memory of the drafting pass — was run against the real source to check for fabrication, cross-skill contradictions, engine duplication, and extension-specific leakage. It caught 6 real, concrete defects, including a hallucinated import and a stale diagram, that the drafting pass had not caught on its own.

Evidence

See the frontmatter evidence field for the full list of 6 defects found and fixed: a fabricated import, a stale directory-layout diagram (in two files), an imprecise count, a broken cross-reference, an overstated capability claim, and a missing section.

What we'd do differently

Not stated this round.

learning.title: A full repo-wide secret scan ahead of an external backup caught a real-looking hardcoded Google API key vendored inside the BaForms third-party PHP source.

fm.learning: A full repo-wide secret scan ahead of an external backup caught a real-looking hardcoded Google API key vendored inside the BaForms third-party PHP source.
fm.evidence: The key was found and redacted from the vendored PHP source, and a repo-wide secret scan run afterward came back clean.
